  logs at ERROR for `jwks_url is missing` after enabling JWT mode
  [mechanism: `ConfigLoader.populateAppHttpConfig` calls `.unwrap()` on a factory that returns
  `success(...)` unconditionally, so there is no failure to propagate; `AppHttpConfig.withSecurityMode`
  constructs the record directly].
- **Residuals from the #902 review, recorded not fixed.** (1) #888 acceptance 2 asked that "no path
  installs `permitAllValidator` where the route's policy is the only gate" be structural; it remains
  conventional — the static factory the javadoc forbids is one `.or(...)` away, and only the grid
  catches a reintroduction. (2) `AppHttpServer.start()` on an already-bound port was reported by the
  stream as returning success; the code as read maps a failed `bind()` to `BindFailed`, so this may
  be a macOS wildcard-bind quirk — unreproduced, check on Linux before filing. (3) The management
  plane's `KvStoreApiKeyValidator` has a dead `BearerTokenRequired -> success(anonymous)` arm and a
  reachable no-header, no-keys `-> success(anonymous VIEWER)` arm (#866 G1 family), and the
  `AetherNode` bootstrap warning states the inverse of that code; all pre-existing, outside this
  diff, filed as #908
  [mechanism: review section 5 and 8 of `review-902-888-2026-09-06`; read-verified, not executed].
- **Other `permitAllValidator` sites, audited.** `AppHttpServerAdapter`'s `NONE` arm is guarded by the
  request-time pre-check that refuses every auth-requiring policy before the validator runs (pinned by
  the `none` row above). `ForgeServer`'s three websocket handlers pass `securityEnabled = false`, the
  documented local-dev case. The management plane already installs `denyUnlessPublicValidator` (#573).
  No other site installs it
  [mechanism: repo-wide grep for `permitAllValidator` and for unconditional `Result.success(SecurityContext`].

### Fixed (2026-09-06 — #886: a block written and never read was invisible to demotion)

- **A block written through the write-through path and never read back now stays a demotion candidate.** Before, `StorageInstance.trackNewBlock` finalized the block by an unconditional `createLifecycle` (a plain map `put`) that replaced the record the cache-tier promotions had just added their presence to, so the metadata named the durable tier alone while the bytes sat in the memory tier. `DefaultDemotionManager.selectCandidates` reads `listBlocksByTier(MEMORY)`, so it could not see the block however far over its high watermark the tier was; only a later read repaired the record, which is why every write-then-read test stayed green. `trackNewBlock` now updates the existing record in place
  [verified: `StorageInstanceWriteOnlyDemotionTest#writeOnly_blocksAreListedUnderMemoryTier` and `#writeOnly_demotionTickMovesBytesOutOfMemory` — six blocks written, none read, a real `DefaultDemotionManager` tick against the instance's own `MetadataStore`; with the production hunk reverted the listing is empty and the tick moves 0 bytes].
- **The mechanism differs from the ticket's, the consequence does not.** The record is not absent when `recordTierPresence` runs: `handlePut` claims the block first (`claimBlock`, a `putIfAbsent` of the initial lifecycle record), and `computeLifecycle`'s `computeIfPresent` applies the cache presence to that claim. What lost it was the overwrite one step later. The claim is therefore treated as THE lifecycle record: it names the tier the active write policy writes first, and finalization is an idempotent add on it, never a re-create. `computeLifecycle` itself is unchanged and still update-only, because `createRef`/`deleteRef` rely on an unknown block staying unknown
  [mechanism: `StorageInstance.sentinelFor`/`initialTier` and `trackNewBlock`; reordering the promotion after finalization was rejected because a cache-tier failure would then leave a real record that `releaseClaim` cannot remove, and a retry would deduplicate into a second refcount instead of rewriting].
- **A reference counted while the write was still in flight now survives finalization.** A second `put` of the same content during the first write's window deduplicates onto the claim (refcount 2, returned as success before the first writer's bytes land). The base re-create replaced that record and dropped the count back to 1, an under-count that would let GC collect a live block once either reference was dropped. Repaired by the same in-place update, not by separate code
  [verified: `StorageInstanceWriteOnlyDemotionTest#writeThrough_duplicatePutWhileWriteInFlight_refCountSurvivesFinalization` — the durable tier's `put` is held open until the duplicate has been counted; with the production hunk reverted the finalized record reads refcount 1].
- **Write-behind was never affected; its record keeps the same tier set and refcount, now pinned to exactly `{MEMORY}`.** Its claim already named the fast tier, so a write-only block was listed under `MEMORY`; the sentinel now names that same tier instead of the durable one, and finalization adds it idempotently. The durable tier is never declared present until a read finds the drained bytes there
  [verified: `StorageInstanceWriteOnlyDemotionTest#writeBehind_writeOnly_blockIsListedUnderFastTier` asserts `presentIn()` is exactly `{MEMORY}` for every block; a sentinel naming the durable tier finalizes as `{MEMORY, LOCAL_DISK}`, declaring disk residency for bytes still queued, and turns the test red].
- **What does change on every finalized record, both policies: `createdAt` and `lastAccessedAt` now carry the claim instant, not the finalization instant.** The record is the claim, so its timestamps are the claim's; the base re-create stamped both again when the write landed. The difference is one write latency, and it shifts `AGE`/`LRU` ordering by that latency and nothing else
  [mechanism: `BlockLifecycle.withTierAdded` copies every field of the record it updates; `sentinelFor` stamps both at claim time].
- **Residuals, stated plainly.** (1) `WriteBehindQueue` never records durable-tier presence when it drains, so a write-behind block's record never gains the durable tier until a read finds it there; pre-existing, not #886, not fixed here. (2) The read path's `recordTierPresence` is also update-only, so a block found in a tier with no local lifecycle record (a shared tier populated by another node, or after a metadata restore) records nothing; no cache fill happens on that path, so nothing becomes invisible to demotion. (3) A successful put still always leaves a record: if the claim vanished mid-write (`restoreLifecycles` clears the map) the fallback re-creates a durable-only record, and that one block is then back in the #886 state, its MEMORY presence unrecorded until a read finds it
  [mechanism: `trackNewBlock`'s `onEmpty` branch; no test drives a restore concurrent with a write].
  (4) On the write-through path a cache-tier `put` failure fails the whole put after the durable write already succeeded, because `flatMap` propagates it; the "skipped" log message on that path describes behavior that does not exist. With two tiers the claim is released and the bytes are orphaned on disk with no record. Pre-existing, not #886, filed separately. (5) A concurrent duplicate `put` returns success from deduplication while the first writer's tier write may still fail; the caller then holds an id whose bytes exist nowhere and whose record survives `releaseClaim` at refcount 2. Pre-existing, not #886. (6) `TierManagementIntegrationTest` still seeds a memory-only lifecycle record directly instead of writing through the instance (its comment names this defect as the reason); whether to convert it is a separate decision, since the instance path also leaves a disk copy and changes what the round trip exercises.
- Supersedes, on this point only, the "reported, not fixed" entry for this defect in the unreleased #783 fragment (`changelog.d/783-content-storage-setup.md`, PR #885)
  [mechanism: that fragment is not on this branch; it and #885's `fillMemoryTier` javadoc describe #886 as current, so whichever PR lands second reconciles the text].

### Fixed (2026-09-06 — #685: the membership-pin await in `StreamOwnerFailoverPinnedTest` was unbounded under a comment claiming it was bounded)

- **`StreamOwnerFailoverPinnedTest.pinMembership` awaited `setAutoHealEnabled(false, …)` — a consensus round-trip since #685 — with a bare `.await()`, directly under a comment reading "Await it, bounded, and fail".** A pin that never resolved would park the `forge-tests` job until the runner's own timeout instead of failing the test by name. The await is now bounded at 30 s; on expiry the existing `onFailure` arm throws with the timeout cause
  [mechanism: `Promise.await(TimeSpan)` returns a failed `Result` on expiry, which the existing `onFailure(cause -> throw new AssertionError(...))` arm converts into a named test failure; the success path is unchanged]. This was #867's one SHOULD-FIX from its review round 1: it was edited in the stream tree but never committed, so #867 merged with the comment and without the code.

### Fixed (2026-09-06 — #268, #891: no provisioned resource was ever closed at slice unload — production `provide()` bypassed the cache, and the default close could not see the project's own close conventions)

- **Every resource provisioned by generated slice code leaked at unload, and `releaseAll` reported success (#268 R1).** Generated code reaches the CONTEXT `provide()` overload; only the plain overload wrote `promiseCache`, so `releaseAll` drained a map nothing had populated and a close was never *attempted*. Both overloads now take one lifecycle path that memoizes the provisioned resource in one map keyed `(type, section, scope)` and releases through it
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$SliceScopedLifecycle#releaseAll_closesResource_provisionedThroughContextOverload`, `#provide_provisionsOnce_whenOneSliceProvidesTwice`; making the context overload bypass the cache again turns 7 of the module's 138 tests red — the list is in the pull request].
- **The context overload is cached PER PROVISIONING SLICE — key `(type, section, sliceId)` — deliberately, not per node.** That overload is codec-scoped: `SliceLoadingContext.CodecAwareResourceProvider` injects the deployed slice's own codec as `Serializer`/`Deserializer` on every call, because it is the only codec that knows the application's record types. A key without a slice dimension would hand slice B the resource slice A built with A's codec, making B's application-typed stream events and DHT entries unencodable — #526 reintroduced by a leak fix. `PublisherFactory` is a second, independent reason: it derives a topic's namespace from the provisioning slice's `Artifact`. Not a behaviour change: the context path was uncached before, and generated code provisions once per slice inside its static create path, so each slice already received its own instance; what is new is that the instance is memoized within the slice and released when that slice unloads. **Recorded consequence: DB connection pools are per-slice, not per-node.** That is today's behaviour, so it is not a regression — a genuinely shared pool is a deliberate design change needing its own ticket, not something to acquire from a cache key
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$CodecScopingSurvivesCaching#secondSlice_receivesItsOwnCodec_notTheFirstSlices` — two slices, same type and section, different codecs; drops the slice dimension and slice-b receives codec-a; `$SliceScopedLifecycle#provide_givesEachSliceItsOwnInstance`, `#releaseAll_closesOnlyTheReleasingSlicesResource`].
- **The plain (context-free) overload keeps its shared `(type, section)` cache, and its resource is never released by any slice's unload.** A plain-overload caller carries no identity the provider can attribute to a slice, so no slice's unload may close its resource — the old code did exactly that, closing a cached resource a plain-path holder still used once the context-path consumer set emptied (#268 R2, use-after-close on a live pool). The unattributed scope is now pinned as a bounded leak, which is the safe direction. **Ruled 2026-09-06 (CTO, `oss/internal/ruling-268-shared-scope-2026-09-06.md`): this scope is process-lifetime.** #268's amended acceptance item 1 asked for refcount and close-on-last-consumer on this path; without a caller identity there is no "last consumer" to count, and the item is rewritten to a node-shutdown close of the shared scope, which is a separate ticket
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$UnattributedScopeIsSharedAndPinned#provide_sharesOneInstance_acrossPlainOverloadCallers`, `#releaseAll_neverCloses_theUnattributedScopesResource` — releasing the unattributed scope's own literal as a slice id also closes nothing].
- **Close goes through the factory that built the resource, not the head of the priority list (#268 R3).** `releaseAll` used `factoryList.getFirst()`; for `SqlConnector`, where the async, R2DBC and JDBC factories all answer and are ordered by priority, that is a different object from the one whose `supports()` matched. The matched factory is now remembered alongside the resource and is the one that closes it
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$ClosesThroughTheProvisioningFactory#releaseAll_closesThroughMatchingFactory_notTheHighestPriorityOne`].
- **A failed provision is no longer memoized (#268 R4).** `computeIfAbsent` cached the failed promise forever, so an `Intermittent` failure the slice-loading FSM retried with backoff handed back the same poisoned promise on every retry. The failing entry now evicts itself and the retry provisions again. The eviction is a DEPENDENT TRANSFORM (`withFailure`) registered ahead of the caller's `map`, so it runs on the resolving thread before any continuation of the caller can observe the failure; as an `onFailure` EVENT it ran after those continuations, and a retry issued from the failure continuation received the memoized failure (review round 1, SF-1: 25 of 50 with the reviewer's probe)
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$FailedProvisioningIsNotMemoized#provide_retryIssuedFromTheFailureContinuation_provisionsAfresh` — the fixture fails ASYNCHRONOUSLY, released only after the retry is chained through `fold`, so the ordering is observable and the event-based eviction fails it every time; `#provide_retriesProvisioning_afterAFailedAttempt` (the factory fails once, synchronously), `SpiResourceProviderTest$Provide#provide_retriesProvisioning_afterAFailedAttempt` (the config loader fails once — the other origin of the same eviction path)].
- **The lifecycle state is ONE map, mutated only through per-key atomics (#268 R5, in part).** It was two — the promise cache and a consumer set per key — updated non-atomically, so a provision racing a release of its own scope could insert into the cache after the release had dropped the set, leaving an entry no release walked (review round 1, SF-2: 187 of 3000 rounds with the reviewer's probe). With the scope in the key that set was always `{scope}` and counted nothing, so it is deleted rather than made atomic. **What is guaranteed now, and by what:** an entry is inserted by `computeIfAbsent` and detached only by `remove(key, value)`, so a provision is linearized against a release of its scope — it either receives the entry the release is about to close (the slice unloading while it provisions: unload wins, exactly as a sequential provide-then-release would) or it creates a fresh entry that the next release of the scope finds. Every entry has exactly one remover and that remover is the one that closes it; nothing is left in the map unreachable by its scope's release. **Not guaranteed:** that a caller racing its own scope's release holds an open resource afterwards — only a lease held for the duration of use could promise that, and the slice-loading FSM sequences create before stop, so the race is not reached in production
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$ProvideRacingReleaseOfTheSameScope#afterEachRacingRound_theNextReleaseClosesWhatTheCallerReceived` — 40,000 rounds of a provision racing two releases of the same scope; after each round one more release must close what the caller received, and at the end no resource is closed twice or left open. Against the two-map code it is red in 5 of 5 runs with 6–20 unreachable rounds per run]. **Not addressed from R5:** partial-provision cleanup — a factory whose `provision` allocates and then fails leaves the allocation behind. Per the #891 audit, 2 of 23 factories unwind today (`JdbcSqlConnectorFactory`, `JdbcJooqConnectorFactory`); `AsyncSqlConnectorFactory` builds a Netty pool and leaks it if the connector constructor throws. That is a per-factory change outside this path.
- **The default close could not see the project's own close convention, and reported success anyway (#891).** `ResourceFactory.close` dispatched on the JDK's `AutoCloseable` only; a resource implementing `AsyncCloseable` (`org.pragmatica.lang.io`, `Promise<Unit> close()`) fell through to `unitPromise()`. Dispatch now recognises `AsyncCloseable` first and awaits its promise, then `AutoCloseable` synchronously; a failed close is absorbed and logged in both branches so one bad resource cannot block the release of the rest. A resource implementing NEITHER is a named outcome (`noCloseConvention`) logged at DEBUG rather than a silent success, so a further convention cannot repeat this quietly
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$DefaultCloseConventionDispatch#releaseAll_closesAsyncCloseableResource_throughDefaultDispatch`, `#releaseAll_stillClosesAutoCloseableResource_throughDefaultDispatch`, `#releaseAll_succeeds_forResourceImplementingNeitherConvention`; dropping the `AsyncCloseable` arm turns 4 of 138 tests red — listed in the pull request. The log line for the neither-convention case is not asserted by any test]. **Stated plainly:** before this change no provisioned resource type implemented `AsyncCloseable`, so this arm changes the behaviour of zero resources by itself; it is what the next two bullets dispatch through.
- **A close that THROWS synchronously cannot abort the release of the other resources.** The default close absorbs a FAILED promise in both branches, but an `AsyncCloseable.close()` or a factory override that throws escaped `releaseAll`'s loop and left every later entry unreleased (review round 1, NOTE 2). `closeThroughOwningFactory` now lifts the throw into a failed promise, logged at WARNING, and `allOf` carries on
  [verified: `SpiResourceProviderLifecycleTest$DefaultCloseConventionDispatch#releaseAll_stillClosesTheOthers_whenOneCloseThrows` — without the guard the exception escapes `releaseAll` itself].
- **All seven `@Sql` connector factories now stop their pools at release.** `DatabaseConnector` declared a THIRD convention, `Promise<Unit> stop()`, and extended neither closeable interface; none of the six concrete connectors (`JdbcSqlConnector`, `PgAsyncSqlConnector`, `R2dbcSqlConnector`, `JdbcJooqConnector`, `R2dbcJooqConnector`, `AsyncJooqConnector`) implements either, so every pool — Hikari, the Netty pg pool, R2DBC — was left open at unload while the close reported success. `DatabaseConnector` now extends `AsyncCloseable` with `close()` delegating to `stop()`: one interface change, zero implementor changes, reaching all seven factories (`db-jdbc`, `db-async` ×2, `db-r2dbc`, `db-jooq`, `db-jooq-async`, `db-jooq-r2dbc`) and the `slice-testkit` fakes that share the interface
  [verified: `DatabaseConnectorCloseTest#releaseAll_stopsTheConnector_throughTheInheritedDefaultClose` — a factory with NO close override, released through the provider, must observe `stop()` having run; `#close_delegatesToStop`; `#connector_isAsyncCloseable_soReleaseDispatchCanSeeIt`. The real connectors' `stop()` overrides are pre-existing and unchanged, and no test in this change drives a real pool].
- **The `@Http` resource is itself `AsyncCloseable`, so releasing it reaches the Netty event loop.** Dispatch sees only the resource OBJECT. `JdkHttpClient` implemented `HttpClient` only and HELD an `HttpOperations` that, with the Netty backend, is the `NettyHttpOperations` owning the `EventLoopGroup` — a closeable one field down is invisible to any dispatch, however wide. `JdkHttpClient` now implements `AsyncCloseable`, closing its operations when they are closeable and succeeding when they are not (the JDK backend owns nothing releasable)
  [verified: `JdkHttpClientCloseTest#close_closesTheOperationsItOwns` — operations supplied through a package-private seam on `JdkHttpClient`, a recording fake implementing `HttpOperations, AsyncCloseable`, its close must have run; replacing `close()` with a unit promise turns it red while `#close_succeeds_withNettyBackend` and `#close_succeeds_withJdkBackend` stay green, so those two pin only that close succeeds; `#client_isAsyncCloseable_soReleaseDispatchCanSeeIt` pins the type for both backends] [mechanism: `NettyHttpOperations.close` calls `eventLoopGroup.shutdownGracefully()` — pre-existing code in `integrations/net/http-client`, not observed by any test here; the thread-count measurement is #895, and see the next heading for why it is blocked].
- **Unattributable claim, retired:** `SpiResourceProviderCompositeTest#provide_withoutCompositeExtension_doesNotEnableCompositePath` asserted that two plain-overload calls returned the same promise; `String.class` has no factory, so what it pinned was a memoized FAILURE (R4 above, as a test expectation). Renamed to `#provide_withoutCompositeExtension_usesConstructorSuppliedLoader` and rewritten to assert the loader routing it is named for.

**Not fixed here — read before expecting a close in production**

- **This change still produces no close on a deployed node.** `releaseAll`'s slice identity can never match a registered consumer: the generated `stop()` passes a two-segment `group:artifact-kebabSlice` coordinate, while registration uses the three-segment `Artifact.asString()` (`group:artifact:version`) — 0 of 34 generated factories on disk can match (**#892**, filed by this work, needs a slice-identity design decision). What lands here is release machinery proven to work when the ids match; it stays inert until #892. **#891's retention measurement (#895) will still show retention after this merges — that is #892, not this fix failing.** A related point for #892's own acceptance: the scope this change keys on is the identity `SliceLoadingContext` registers, so two slices deployed from one artifact share one cache entry and one consumer identity, and the first of them to unload closes the shared resource while the other still holds it. Before this change nothing closed at all, so it is not a regression, but it is the same identity question #892 must settle.
- **Two factory-level `close` overrides remain silent no-ops:** `@Notify`'s `NotificationSenderFactory` (**#271**, leaks the SMTP event loop) and `ContentStoreFactory` (**#893**). Both bypass the default dispatch fixed here and are untouched.
- **`CacheInterceptorFactory` and `IdempotencyInterceptorFactory` retain registries on the FACTORY** that no release path prunes (**#894**, pull request #898 open) — the one leak that survives every fix above because the state is not on the resource.
- **Partial-provision cleanup** (R5, above) and **the plain overload's bounded leak** (R2, above) are recorded, not fixed.
- **Review round 1 residuals, not fixed:** a context call carrying a codec but no slice-id extension would land in the shared scope with its codec — no production path builds one, `DependencyResolver` always supplies the artifact id (review NOTE 3); `releaseAll` walks every cache entry, O(entries) per release (NOTE 7); two slices deployed from one artifact share one scope, which is #892's identity question (NOTE 1).
- No other unreleased fragment touches `SpiResourceProvider`, `ResourceFactory`, `DatabaseConnector` or `releaseAll`; nothing to reconcile.

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #877: storage read cache could hand a fresh reader someone else's stale timeout)
- **A caller of `StorageInstance.get()` could receive a PREVIOUS attempt's failure instead of a
  fresh load**, because `SingleFlightCache.deduplicate()`'s eviction (`onResultRun` removing the
  settled map entry) dispatches asynchronously, off-thread
  [mechanism: `PromiseImpl.processActions` submits `onResultRun` completions via
  `AsyncExecutor.INSTANCE.runAsync`, which returns before the removal executes — unordered relative
  to a blocked `.await()` waking up]. For the whole window between a promise resolving and its
  eviction actually running, the map still held the stale, already-settled promise; any caller of
  `deduplicate()` for that `BlockId` — not only a thread that was itself blocked in `.await()` —
  landing in that window hit `computeIfAbsent`'s stale entry and inherited its result. When the
  previous attempt was a hung loader that had hit its in-flight bound, the new caller inherited that
  `CoreError.Timeout`, defeating the bound's own purpose (unstopping subsequent readers). Reachable
  in production: `StorageInstance.get()` routes every real block read through `deduplicate()`
  concurrently and non-blockingly, exactly the near-simultaneous-readers pattern the cache exists to
  coalesce; the window widens under carrier contention, i.e. worse exactly under the load where the
  cache matters most.
- `deduplicate()` now uses `compute` instead of `computeIfAbsent` and treats an existing-but-
  resolved map entry as absent, so a settled entry can never be handed out regardless of whether the
  async cleanup has run yet — this closes the race instead of narrowing it
  [verified: `SingleFlightCacheTest$HungLoaderEvictionTests#deduplicate_hungLoader_nextCallerFreshEvenWithCleanupQueuedBehindSaturatedCarriers`,
  which busy-spins exactly `jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism` virtual threads to hold every
  carrier hostage before the bound fires, forcing the cleanup dispatch to still be queued when the
  next caller arrives — 5/5 deterministic FAIL against the pre-fix `computeIfAbsent`, 5/5
  deterministic PASS against this fix, both ~0.17-0.19s (no wall-clock race or ambient-load
  dependence in either direction); `deduplicate_hungLoader_evictedAfterBoundAndNextCallerFresh`
  covers the same eviction contract without forcing the race window].
- **Adversarial review of this same fix found a second, distinct defect it introduced**: treating a
  resolved entry as absent (above) means a settled promise A's map slot can legitimately be
  superseded by a fresh promise B for the same id before A's own asynchronous cleanup runs. The
  original cleanup removed by key only (`inFlight.remove(id)`), which deletes whatever currently
  occupies the slot — after supersession, that is B, a live in-flight promise, not the settled A
  that scheduled the removal. A subsequent caller then finds the slot empty and starts a third,
  duplicate load, silently breaking the single-flight guarantee itself under exactly the churn this
  fix targets (each caller still resolves correctly from its own promise reference, so nothing
  looks wrong from the outside). Fixed by removing with the atomic two-argument
  `inFlight.remove(id, promise)` (compare-and-remove), a no-op once the slot no longer holds the
  promise that scheduled the cleanup
  [verified: `SingleFlightCacheTest$HungLoaderEvictionTests#deduplicate_liveSuccessorSurvives_predecessorsDelayedCleanup`,
  which reuses the carrier-saturation harness to hold A's cleanup pending while B is created and
  kept deliberately unresolved, then releases the carriers and — via an observer chained onto A's
  own promise, guaranteed by same-promise completion ordering to fire only after the cache's own
  cleanup has run — waits for proof the cleanup actually executed before asserting a third caller
  joins B rather than starting a third load: 5/5 deterministic FAIL against the key-only
  `remove(id)` (real assertion failure, not a timeout), 5/5 deterministic PASS against
  `remove(id, promise)`; full-class regression 7/7 testcases, 0 failures/errors].
- **Honest limit on the claim:** this was found while chasing #859, an intermittently failing test
  (`SingleFlightCacheTest$HungLoaderEvictionTests.deduplicate_hungLoader_evictedAfterBoundAndNextCallerFresh`,
  "Expected fresh load to succeed: Promise timed out after 150ms") — the failure message is
  *consistent with* a previous attempt's `Timeout` resurfacing, but the race did not reproduce under
  ambient CI-like load in 40+ attempts across two independent investigations (raw CPU pressure,
  carrier-parallelism pinned to 1, host busy-loops). The causal link between this defect and the
  #859 CI failures is therefore **not proven, only consistent**. This fix closes a real window on
  its own merits, independent of whether it explains #859; whether the CI flake also disappears is
  a prediction to be confirmed by CI staying green over subsequent runs, not asserted as fact here.
  #859's test asserts a single-shot fresh load and needs no wall-clock poll once this race is
  closed — it is fixed as a consequence, not with a separate change.

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #874: DHT writes could reach the tier before admission; #875: a refused admission check never resolved the gate)
- **A write reaching a DHT-backed storage instance during the marker-check window could persist
  plaintext into a namespace the check later finds already encrypted.** #858's admission latch
  (`DhtStorageTier.readGate`, resolved post-formation by `StorageFactory.verifyDhtMarker`) gated `get`
  only, reasoning only a read could observe a not-yet-verified namespace. That missed two things:
  `AetherNode.start()` brings `managementServer`/`appHttpServer` up *before* `verifyDhtMarkers()` runs,
  so an ungated `put` reachable over HTTP (e.g. a Maven `deploy`) could write ahead of the check; and
  `exists` is itself a DHT round trip, not a local, gate-free check. `put`, `delete` and `exists` are
  now gated on the same `readGate` as `get` — no operation can reach the DHT tier ahead of admission.
  Because the DHT is a cluster-wide shared store (`DhtStorageTier#isShared`), a write that landed ahead
  of the check would have replicated to peers and survived this node's own subsequent
  `EncryptedTierRequiresKeyring` abort; this closes that window without changing `AetherNode`'s startup
  ordering, since every DHT operation — not just HTTP-surface timing — is now the enforcement point.
- **A refused admission check left the gate unresolved, so a caller racing it waited the full 30 s
  `admissionTimeout` and saw the wrong error.** `StorageFactory.verifyDhtMarker` resolved `readGate`
  only on success (`.onSuccess(...)`); its failure branch (no keyring, marker already present) left
  `readGate` pending. A reader/writer arriving during that window timed out with
  `StorageError.TierNotAdmitted` instead of the real refusal cause
  (`EncryptionError.EncryptedTierRequiresKeyring`). The failure branch now resolves the same gate with
  the refusal cause, so a racing caller fails immediately with the real cause instead of waiting out
  the bound.
- `configuration.md`'s DHT-marker-timing section corrected: it previously claimed the check runs
  "before the node reports ready", which reads as if HTTP surfaces wait for it. They don't — what
  blocks during that window is every DHT-tier operation on the pending namespace, not the HTTP surface.
- **Round 1 (review) fix — the #875 regression test could not fail, it could only wedge.**
  `verifyDhtMarker_resolvesReadGate_withRefusalCause_onProductionFailurePath` ended in an unbounded
  `c.readGate().await()`; a regression on `StorageFactory.verifyDhtMarker`'s failure branch
  (dropping `check.readGate().resolve(Result.failure(cause))`) would hang the test forever instead of
  failing it — `readGate` is independent of `DhtStorageTier`'s `admissionTimeout` (that bound applies
  only to the `.map()`-derived promise inside `DhtStorageTier#admission`, never to `readGate` itself),
  so the comment claiming a 30 s production bound would eventually rescue it was false. Now bounded
  with the file's existing `SHORT_MARKER_TIMEOUT` (150 ms); the false comment is replaced with the
  correct mechanism. Proved by mutation: reverting the two-line fix makes the test fail in ~11s
  wall-clock with a real assertion (`CoreError.Timeout` where `EncryptionError.EncryptedTierRequiresKeyring`
  was expected), not a hang; restoring the fix returns it to a 0.28s pass.
- **Round 1 (review) fix — a gated write/read answered HTTP 500, not 503.**
  `StorageError.TierNotAdmitted` is not a `CoreError.Timeout`, so `MavenProtocolRoutes.sendFailureResponse`
  fell through to `internalError` (500) for a state that is transient by construction — telling
  `mvn deploy` "server bug, do not retry" instead of "retry me". `TierNotAdmitted` now maps to 503
  Service Unavailable with a `Retry-After: 1` header; every other cause is unaffected and still gets 500.
- [verified: `DhtStorageTierTest$Admission` (six `@Test` methods: pending-gate-timeout and
  immediate-refusal cases for `get`/`put`/`delete`/`exists`, including two that assert directly against
  the raw DHT client that a gated write never persists, whether it times out or is refused) — 6/6, read
  from surefire `<testcase>` counts (not the `.txt` summary, which undercounts `@Nested` classes);
  `StorageFactoryEncryptionTest#verifyDhtMarker_resolvesReadGate_withRefusalCause_onProductionFailurePath`
  (drives the real no-keyring-refusal path through `StorageFactory.verifyDhtMarker` and reads
  `readGate()` directly, without resolving it by hand; mutation-probed per above) — 1/1;
  `MavenProtocolRoutesTierNotAdmittedTest` (503+`Retry-After` for `TierNotAdmitted`, plain 500 with no
  `Retry-After` for every other cause) — 2/2;
  `aether/aether-storage` MODULE suite (full, `mvn -pl aether/aether-storage test`) — 30/30;
  `aether/node` MODULE suite (full, `mvn -pl aether/node test`, not a reactor total — no full-monorepo
  reactor run was performed this round since only `aether/node` sources changed) — 1138/1138, 1 skipped
  (pre-existing, unrelated to this change);
  `mvn jbct:check -pl aether/node -fae` — 0 format issues, 0 lint errors (aether-storage source is
  unchanged this round, not re-gated)]
- **What is NOT covered:** `AetherNode.start()`'s startup ordering is unchanged — `managementServer`/
  `appHttpServer` still come up before `verifyDhtMarkers()` resolves; protection now comes from gating
  every DHT-tier operation rather than delaying HTTP-surface startup, which was weighed and rejected
  because it would delay unrelated, non-DHT HTTP traffic (health checks, other endpoints) for up to the
  full 30 s bound. `Promise.allOfOrCancel` in `StorageFactory.verifyDhtMarkers` (plural) cancels
  sibling in-flight marker checks on the first failure; the exact cancellation cause a cancelled
  sibling's `readGate` now resolves with is a strict improvement over the pre-#875 hang but its precise
  type is unverified here. The `Retry-After: 1` value is a deliberately small, unmeasured hint
  [design intent — unverified], not a measured recovery-time bound.

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #858: DHT encryption-marker check moved off the boot path)
- **Every boot with a DHT-backed storage instance and no keyring hung for 30 s, then aborted.**
  `StorageFactory.createAll` — called from the `AetherNode` constructor, before cluster formation —
  awaited a DHT get/put (`refuseIfDhtEncryptedWithoutKeyring`/`writeDhtMarker`, the reverse-direction
  guard from #253/#830) against a `DistributedDHTClient` that can only route once `start()`'s cluster
  formation resolves. The construction-time DHT operation could never complete: every real boot with a
  DHT tier failed `"Failed to create storage '<name>'"` after the full `DHT_MARKER_TIMEOUT`. #830's own
  tests never caught this because they exercise `InMemoryDHTClient`, which answers immediately with no
  cluster to form.
- **The DHT marker check now runs from `start()`, after cluster formation resolves and before the node
  reports ready**, generically over every DHT-backed storage instance `StorageFactory` assembles (not a
  hardcoded list — covers `artifacts`, any `[storage.<name>]` instance, and #783's future `content`
  routing through the same path once merged). Construction itself now never touches the DHT: it stages
  a `DhtMarkerCheck` (instance name, DHT key prefix, keyring key id if any) per DHT tier and returns
  immediately. Two outcomes, same fail-closed causes as before, just later:
  - No keyring, marker present on the DHT tier → `start()` fails with `EncryptedTierRequiresKeyring`
    (identical cause to the pre-existing disk-side check, which is unchanged — a disk read needs no
    cluster and stays synchronous during construction).
  - Keyring configured → the marker is written for real once formation resolves, bounded by the same
    30 s timeout; a wedged DHT now fails `start()` with a distinct `DhtMarkerCheckTimedOut` cause
    instead of masquerading as the disk-side refusal.
  A DHT tier serves no reads until its own check completes (gated internally on `DhtStorageTier`, not
  a separate config knob). A boot that fails either cause stops the node the same way any other
  `start()` failure does: exit code `1` (`Main#exitWithError`).
  **Superseded in part by #1052, same release:** `DhtMarkerCheckTimedOut` no longer fails `start()`. It
  is retried with backoff while the tier stays gated and the node stays not-ready. Only
  `EncryptedTierRequiresKeyring` still exits.
- [verified: `StorageFactoryEncryptionTest#createAll_leavesNoDhtMarker_whenDiskGuardRefusesBeforeDhtEncryptionIsApplied`,
  `#verifyDhtMarker_fails_whenDhtCarriesEncryptionMarker_andDiskUnavailable_andNoKeyringSupplied`,
  `#verifyDhtMarker_fails_withDhtMarkerCheckTimedOut_whenDhtClientNeverResponds` (pins a DHT client
  whose get/put never resolve — construction completes without awaiting it; red-before against the
  reverted hunk hangs ~30 s) — 16/16;
  `DhtStorageTierTest` — 11/11;
  `AetherNodeDhtMarkerPostFormationBootTest#construction_staysUnderFiveSeconds_whenArtifactsInstanceHasDhtTierButNoKeyring`,
  `#start_writesDhtMarkerPostFormation_absentBeforePresentAfter_readThroughNodesOwnDhtClient` — real,
  self-forming single-node boot through `AetherNode.start()`, marker read back off the node's own
  `DHTClient`, absent before formation and present with the active key id after — 2/2;
  `EmberClusterForeignAdmissionTest` — 4/4 (regression guard: unaffected by this change, re-run because
  it forms a real cluster through the same `createNode`/`start()` path);
  `aether/node` full module suite — 1135/1135;
  `mvn jbct:check -pl aether/node,aether/aether-storage` — 0 format issues, 0 lint errors, clean on
  both touched modules;
  `./forge.sh ci` — 16/16 classes, 48 tests, 0 failures/errors, 1 expected skip (the acceptance
  instrument named in #858 — the pre-fix baseline errors 15/16 in `@BeforeAll` on the same suite)]
- **What is NOT covered:** the disk-side marker guards (#253/#830) are unchanged — they run
  synchronously during storage construction because a local-disk read needs no cluster, and this fix
  does not move them. #783's `content` instance is still routed through a separate, keyring-less
  factory path (`StorageFactory.defaultContentStorage`) and is not yet subject to either marker check;
  when #783 merges `content` through `createAll`, it inherits this post-formation check automatically
  — no hardcoded per-instance list to update. The `stream-segments` DHT namespace gap tracked as #849
  is untouched by this fix.
