### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #772: a route expecting a JSON body answered 500 for a missing or malformed body)

- **A missing, empty, or malformed request body on a route declared with `.withBody(...)` fell through to the framework's `ErrorMapper.defaultMapper()` 500 fallback instead of a client-error response** — Jackson's binding failure (`JsonError.TypeMismatch`/`InvalidJson`/etc.) was a plain `Cause`, never an `HttpError`, so nothing distinguished "the client sent a bad body" from an unexpected server fault. `RequestContext` now exposes `jsonBody(TypeToken<T>)`, wrapping every body-parsing failure as `HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST.with(cause)` — mirroring the existing `PathParameter#mapped` (#397) pattern — and all twelve `withBody` combinators in `Route` route through it. The RFC 9457 problem body's `detail` names the expected type, taken directly from the underlying `JsonError` message
  [verified: `aether/http-routing-adapter/src/test/java/org/pragmatica/aether/http/adapter/SliceRouterJsonBodyTest.java` — real `SliceRouter`/`HttpRequestContext` dispatch, missing/malformed/valid bodies].
- A body that PARSES successfully but fails domain validation performed by the handler itself is unaffected by this fix and still answers 500 today — the handler's own `Cause` is never an `HttpError`
  [verified: `SliceRouterJsonBodyTest#postItem_returns500_whenBodyParsesButHandlerRejectsDomainValidation`].
- **Cosmetic**: `JsonError.TypeMismatch`'s message carried a dangling `" at "` suffix for a root-level/pathless mismatch (Jackson's `getPathReference()` returns `""`, not `null`, so the null-only `Option.option` filter left it present) — most visible on exactly this bug's missing-body case. `typeMismatch(...)` now also filters a blank path
  [verified: `SliceRouterJsonBodyTest#postItem_returns400_namingExpectedType_whenBodyMissing`].
- Docs updated: HTTP adapter reference — status codes for missing/malformed request bodies.

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #763: a route declared `public` was treated as undeclared and inherited the global auth policy)

- **Action required if you run `security_mode = "api-key"` or `"jwt"`.** A route whose `routes.toml`
  has no `[security]` section used to answer `200` unauthenticated; after this fix it inherits the
  global `security_mode` and answers `401`/`403` instead (that is the defect this ticket fixes — see
  the next bullet). 16 non-test `routes.toml` files in this repo are in that state today, all under
  `examples/` and `aether/e2e-tests/`. Add `[security]` / `default = "public"` to any of them whose
  routes must stay open. `security_mode = "none"` deployments are unaffected.
- **A route with no `[security]` section at all could not be distinguished, at request time, from one explicitly declared `default = "public"`** — `RouteConfigLoader` collapsed both cases to `RouteSecurityLevel.PUBLIC` during codegen, so `AppHttpServer`'s `isExplicitPolicy` check had nothing left to key off. The ticket's own cite (`AppHttpServer.isExplicitPolicy`) was not wrong, only incomplete — the actual defaulting happened one layer earlier, in codegen. `RouteSecurityLevel`/`SecurityPolicy` gained a third state, `Unspecified`, distinct from `Public` and `Authenticated`: an undeclared route now inherits the server's global policy (auth required when the global policy requires it), an explicitly `public` route bypasses the global policy for exactly that route, and an explicitly authenticated route is unchanged
  [verified: `aether/node/src/test/java/org/pragmatica/aether/http/AppHttpServerRouteSecurityPolicyTest.java` — real `AppHttpServer` in API_KEY mode, three states, real `HttpClient`].
- `Unspecified` is a compile-time/codegen-only concept — no route is ever SERVED carrying it; resolution to a concrete policy happens once, at registration
  [mechanism: `RouteMetadataExtractor.resolveSecurityPolicy` resolves before the route reaches the server; an unresolved value reaching request time would fail closed to "inherit the global policy", never "public" — no such path exists today].
- **A second site carried the same defect**: `RouteMetadataExtractorImpl.resolveSecurityPolicy`, used for hand-written/programmatic routes rather than codegen-produced ones, also defaulted an undeclared route to `publicRoute()` instead of `unspecified()`. Fixed and pinned by its own test
  [verified: `aether/aether-invoke/src/test/java/org/pragmatica/aether/http/RouteMetadataExtractorSecurityPolicyTest.java`].
- **Two of the three HTTP security validators had a fail-open `default` arm**, not merely a non-exhaustive one: `ApiKeySecurityValidator` and `JwtSecurityValidator` granted access unconditionally for any policy value their explicit `case`s didn't name — in practice reachable only by the `Unspecified` sentinel or a dead placeholder type, since every real policy constant is already handled by an explicit case. Unreachable in production (the server resolves `Unspecified` away before dispatch), but a fail-open trap for any direct caller. The `default` arm is now **deleted, not merely denied** — both switches are exhaustive over the sealed `SecurityPolicy` hierarchy with an explicit `Unspecified` case returning a new `SecurityError.UNRESOLVED_POLICY`, so the next constant anyone adds is a compile error rather than a silent fail-open
  [verified: `ApiKeySecurityValidatorTest#validate_denies_forUnspecifiedPolicy`, `JwtSecurityValidatorTest$PolicyVariantTests#validate_denies_forUnspecifiedPolicy`; compile-time exhaustiveness — removing either validator's `Unspecified` case no longer compiles].
  A third validator, `KvStoreApiKeyValidator`, has a structurally different default arm (delegates to a real credential check, matching the existing documented "unconfigured = open" pattern) and was deliberately left unchanged.
- **`SecurityOverrideApplier`'s `strengthen_only` check was meaningless on undeclared routes**: it compared `newPolicy.strength()` against the route's raw declared strength, and `Unspecified`'s is `-1` — so any override, including a downgrade to `public` (strength `0`), passed the "strengthen only" check. The applier cannot see the deployment's global security mode at publish time (`aether-invoke` does not depend on `aether-config`), so it cannot compute the route's true effective strength. It now judges only the DIRECTION of the change on such a route: an override to `public` is refused (it is the floor under every global mode, so it can only weaken); every other override is applied
  [verified: `SecurityOverrideApplierTest$StrengthenOnlyPolicyTests` — `unspecified -> public` rejected, `unspecified -> authenticated` and `unspecified -> role:admin` applied; reverting the guard turns the latter two red].
- **Scope limit on the above — an accepted override does not govern every request, and this release does not change that.** "Applied" means the override reaches the route's replicated entry: that is what `GET /api/v1/routes` reports, and what **other** nodes resolve and enforce before forwarding. It does **not** reach the local authorization decision on the node HOSTING the route, which reads the route's declared (pre-override) policy. A request arriving directly at the hosting node is therefore authorized by the declared policy — or by the global `security_mode` if the route declared none — while the routes listing shows the override in effect. Nodes are individually addressable, so enforcement depends on which node the client reaches. **This mis-plumbing is pre-existing, is not introduced or closed here, and is tracked as #887.** Until it is closed, do not rely on a security override as the only control on a sensitive route; declare the policy in the slice's `routes.toml` as well
  [mechanism: `HttpRoutePublisher` writes raw routes into `publishedRoutes` and applies overrides into a local `effectiveRoutes` used only to build the KV entry; `findLocalRoute` reads `publishedRoutes`, and the node's own entry is excluded from its own `remoteRoutes` by identity].
- **Known residuals on the above, stated plainly — three, not one.** (1) Under `security_mode = "api-key"` (the default), an override to `authenticated` (strength `10`) on an undeclared route whose effective policy is `ApiKeyRequired` (strength `20`) is a weakening this rule still permits. (2) The identical weakening exists under `security_mode = "jwt"`, where the effective policy is `BearerTokenRequired`, also strength `20`; `SecurityMode` has exactly three constants, so (1) and (2) cover the whole enforcing set and only `none` is unaffected. (3) A credential-**type** mismatch is not a strength weakening at all — `bearer_token` and `api_key` both score `20` — so it is invisible to the ordering; see the next bullet. Closing (1) and (2) requires the override path to know the global security mode, a design change deferred past rc4. Declare `[security]` explicitly on any route where the distinction matters
  [design intent — unverified: no test covers residuals (1) and (2), because the current code permits them by construction].
- **Security-critical: an override to a credential type the node cannot serve was a total authentication bypass.** `ApiKeySecurityValidator` returned SUCCESS with an anonymous, unauthenticated context — no credential inspected — for a `BEARER_TOKEN` policy, and `JwtSecurityValidator` did the same for an `API_KEY` policy. Neither value can be declared in `routes.toml` (`RouteSecurityLevel` parses only `public`/`authenticated`/`role:*`/`unspecified`) and neither can be produced by `globalSecurityPolicy()`, which only ever yields the policy matching the mode — so their sole producer is an **operator security override**. Under the default `api-key` mode, an operator overriding a route to `bearer_token` — which reads as a lock-down, and which `GET /api/v1/routes` then reports as `BEARER_TOKEN` — served that route to anyone. Both arms now deny with `SecurityError.UNENFORCEABLE_POLICY` (`401`): the node refuses what it cannot enforce rather than serving it wide open
  [verified: `ApiKeySecurityValidatorTest#validate_denies_forBearerTokenPolicy_thisNodeCannotEnforceIt` and `#..._evenWithAValidApiKeyPresented`, `JwtSecurityValidatorTest#validate_denies_forApiKeyRequiredPolicy_thisNodeCannotEnforceIt` and `#..._evenWithAValidTokenPresented`. The two tests these replace asserted the bypass as intended behaviour ("wrong validator type passes through", `isAuthenticated() == false`)].
- **Action required if any route carries a credential-type policy that does not match the node's `security_mode`.** The fix above is a behaviour change for a real configuration, not only for an attack: a route whose effective policy is `bearer_token` on a node running `security_mode = "api-key"` (or `api_key` on a `jwt` node) **used to return `200` and now returns `401`**. Requests that worked yesterday will start failing on upgrade. This is not a regression — that route was never checking anything, so every one of those `200`s was served to an unauthenticated caller; the previous behaviour was the defect and the `401` is the correction. **The only way to reach this state is an operator security override in `blueprint.toml`**, since `routes.toml` cannot declare either value and the global policy always matches the mode. **What to do:** find any override naming `api_key` or `bearer_token` (`GET /api/v1/routes` reports the effective value per route) and either change it to match the node's `security_mode`, or change it to `authenticated`, which means "any valid credential this node accepts" and resolves to whichever type the mode serves. Changing `security_mode` to match the override works too, but affects every route on the node
  [verified: the mode x policy grid — under `security_mode = "none"` nothing changes, because `AppHttpServer` rejects every non-`public` effective policy with `NO_VALIDATOR_CONFIGURED` before any validator is reached; under `api-key` and `jwt` exactly one cell each changes, and it is the mismatched credential type. Every other cell — `public`, `authenticated`, `role:*`, and the matching credential type — is byte-for-byte unchanged].
- **A remote node's route could govern a local route's security decision.** Policy lookup consulted remote routes whenever the LOCAL route carried no explicit policy — but remote matching is by PREFIX, and `computeRouteTable` excludes a remote route only on exact `method:pathPrefix` identity. With `Public` now an adoptable explicit policy, a broader remote prefix (`/api/v1/pricing/`) could supply a `public` policy to a narrower undeclared local path (`/api/v1/pricing/analytics/`) and the local route would be served with no credential. This is reachable in the partially-migrated state this very changelog's "action required" instructions produce — parent slice migrated, child not yet. A matched LOCAL route now governs its own policy outright: `Unspecified` means "inherit the global policy", never "ask a remote node". Dispatch was already local-first, so the policy decision now agrees with the route that actually serves the request
  [verified: `AppHttpServerRouteSecurityPolicyTest#dispatch_doesNotAdoptRemotePolicy_whenLocalRouteMatchedButUndeclared` — live `AppHttpServer`, real `HttpRouteRegistry` carrying a remote public parent prefix; reverting the hunk turns 401 into 200].
- **`SecurityPolicy.asString()` and `strength()` kept fail-soft `default` arms** (`default -> "API_KEY"`, `default -> 20`) while the validators two methods away had theirs deleted. `SecurityPolicy` is sealed over seven records and both switches covered six, so the arms were live, not dead: a newly added state would have been silently persisted to the KV store as `"API_KEY"` and scored `20` — a fabricated wire value and a fabricated strength, on the override-comparison and cross-node resolution paths. Both `default` arms are removed and every case is handled explicitly. The one remaining subtype, the `unused()` placeholder, is handled with values chosen to fail CLOSED — `strength()` returns `Integer.MAX_VALUE` so the override applier refuses every override on such a route, and `asString()` returns `"UNUSED"`, which `fromString` deliberately does not recognize, so a reader falls to `apiKeyRequired()` and logs. It has no construction site today but is **not** unconstructable: Java gives interface member types implicit `public` and a record's canonical constructor must be at least as accessible as the record, so it cannot be sealed off
  [verified: adding a new sealed state fails compilation at both switches ("the switch expression does not cover all possible input values"); restoring the `default` arms makes that same state compile silently].
- **`SecurityPolicy.fromString`'s `"UNSPECIFIED"` case had no test** and could be deleted with the whole suite green. Without it, an `UNSPECIFIED` entry read back from a remote node falls through `parseRoleOrDefault` to `apiKeyRequired()` — an explicit policy, which is then adopted instead of the global fallback
  [verified: `SecurityValueObjectsTest#fromString_unspecifiedDeserialization` and `#fromString_unspecifiedRoundTrip_throughAsString`; deleting the case turns both red].
- **Mixed-version wire note — read before upgrading.** `NodeRoutesValue.RouteEntry.security` is a persisted `String` whose value domain gains `"UNSPECIFIED"`. A node running an older build lacks the `fromString` case, falls through `parseRoleOrDefault`, and resolves the value to `apiKeyRequired()`. That is fail-closed in DIRECTION — the route demands a credential rather than becoming public — but it is a behaviour change across versions: the older node enforces `api_key` on a route whose owner declared nothing and expected the global policy. **This is not a statement that mixed-version clusters are safe.** Aether does not support rolling upgrades (#666/#434: no join-time version check, no wire negotiation); the supported path is full-cluster stop, upgrade, start. Recorded here because the value domain changed, not because a mixed-version cluster is sanctioned
  [mechanism: `SecurityPolicy.parseRoleOrDefault` returns `apiKeyRequired()` for any unrecognized value; see `aether/docs/reference/known-limitations.md`].
- **Round-trip gap**: codegen's `RouteSecurityLevel.toConfigString()` could emit `"unspecified"` into the generated manifest, but `RouteSecurityLevel.parse()` had no matching case and would fail with "Unknown security level: unspecified". Added the missing case. Also operator-visible: `GET /api/v1/routes` and the dashboard now report `UNSPECIFIED` (not `PUBLIC`) for a route with no `[security]` section
  [verified: `RouteSecurityLevelTest` — parse/toConfigString round trip for all four states].
- Docs updated: HTTP adapter reference — `PUBLIC` declaration semantics and the three-state resolution.

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #685: auto-heal disable was in-memory only and silently reverted on leader failover)
- **An operator's `aether cluster topology auto-heal disable` (#603) lived only in the leader process's `AtomicBoolean`.** A leader failover silently re-enabled auto-heal: the newly-elected leader's fresh `ClusterTopologyManager` never saw the previous leader's in-memory flag, and `status` answered from that same volatile copy — an operator could disable auto-heal, watch `status` confirm it, and have it revert with no error and no audit trail the moment leadership moved.
- **The disable/enable decision is now a durable cluster fact**, written as a typed `AutoHealStateKey`/`AutoHealStateValue` record through the same consensus-backed command path as other topology mutations, and read through on every `isAutoHealEnabled()`/`status` call instead of cached in memory [mechanism: `KVStore.getTyped` read-through; unit-proven by `ClusterTopologyManagerAutoHealDurabilityTest` — two independent `ClusterTopologyManager` instances over one shared `KVStore`, one disabling while the other, which never received the call, observes the disable and, later, the re-enable]. An absent key (a fresh cluster, or one that predates #685) answers enabled, preserving the pre-#685 default.
- **Staleness is explicit, not implied:** a read reflects the log applied LOCALLY; the disable becomes visible on a node when that node applies the committed Put — bounded by consensus latency, not zero; a node behind on apply answers the previous value until then.
- `setAutoHealEnabled` now returns `Promise<Boolean>` (prior state) instead of a synchronous `boolean`, reflecting that the write is a consensus round-trip, not a local mutation. A same-state call still writes through to the KV even when the requested value matches the prior one — the request is answered from this node's local view, which may be stale, so the write stays unconditional (#685 review round 1).

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #654: cursor commits on consumer detach and checkpoint were discarded unobserved)

- **`ConsumerRuntimeState.flushCursorForKey` called `ConsumerCursorStore.commit(...)` — a consensus write — and dropped the returned `Promise<Unit>` unobserved**: no await, no failure log, no counter, no retry. This ran on every consumer detach and inside node stop's #488 ordering window, so a failed final commit before shutdown was invisible. `checkpointIfNeeded`'s periodic commit had the same defect and is fixed the same way.
- **`close()` now bound-awaits every final commit**: `awaitFinalCursorCommits()` collects one `Promise<Unit>` per attached consumer and calls `Promise.allOf(commits).await(CURSOR_COMMIT_SHUTDOWN_BOUND)` with a 5-second bound; node stop always continues past the bound, it never blocks on a wedged consensus write [mechanism: `Promise.allOf` derives its own aggregate promise and `.await(TimeSpan)` on timeout returns a manufactured `Timeout` result without cancelling or resolving the underlying commits — the late result still lands on whichever handlers are attached]. Every commit still unresolved the instant the bound expires is reported individually by `reportIfUnsettled`, not as one aggregate: it increments the node-wide `cursorCommitFailureCount` counter, records the per-partition detail (`unsettled at shutdown bound`), and logs once at ERROR naming that consumer group/stream/partition — the same per-commit surface a genuine failure uses, not a single WARNING naming the whole pending batch.
- **Both paths route through `observedCommit`**, which attaches `onSuccess`/`onFailure` to the commit promise: success clears the consumer's recorded failure, failure increments a new node-wide `cursorCommitFailureCount` counter, records the per-partition detail, and logs once at ERROR with group/stream/partition [verified: `StreamConsumerRuntimeTest.CursorCommitObservability`, 4 tests, plus two surgical single-hunk mutation probes — stripping the handler attachment and stripping the bound-await each failed exactly the predicted subset of tests].
- **Surfaced through the existing read surface, not a new one**: `StreamConsumerRuntime.cursorCommitFailureCount()` (new interface method, node-wide, survives detach) and `SubscriptionSnapshot.lastCursorCommitFailure` (new 7th field, per-consumer, cleared on detach). On the Management API, `DeclarativeConsumerPartition` gained a `lastCursorCommitFailure` field rather than overloading `DeclarativeConsumerDetail.diagnostic` — `diagnostic` is per-consumer and already multiplexes several unrelated health conditions (unassigned partitions, non-publishable event type), while a cursor commit failure is per-partition; folding it in would have lost both the partition granularity and the ability to tell which condition fired when more than one applies. The new field follows the same empty-string-for-absent convention.
- **Redelivery contract documented** in `management-api.md` beside the new fields: a commit that never lands past the shutdown bound is retried the same way any restart replays a partition — from the last durably committed cursor, so at-least-once delivery holds and the operator's recovery signal is the counter/detail staying non-zero, not a thrown error [design intent — unverified against a live multi-node failure injection; the bound and counter are exercised, the end-to-end redelivery-after-timeout path is not].
- **Round 2: the production `ClusterCursorStore` (#488) resolved `commit(...)` on the local disk write alone** — the consensus checkpoint publish that actually makes a cursor visible after failover was fire-and-forget, its failure swallowed at DEBUG, so round 1's entire observability surface above never observed the write the ticket named. `ClusterCursorStore.commit` now chains the publish onto the same `Promise` (`local.commit(...).flatMap(_ -> publishCheckpoint(...))`), keeping #488's rule that a consensus failure must never fail the local checkpoint by recovering the publish failure into a successful `Unit` rather than propagating it — but the failure is no longer discarded: it is recorded (keyed by consumer group/stream/partition) and logged once at WARN, and the 5-second shutdown bound at close now covers the publish leg too, not just the local write [mechanism: `flatMap` chains the publish onto `commit(...)`'s own Promise, so `Promise.await(TimeSpan)`'s existing timeout-without-cancel behavior bounds it the same way it already bounded the local write].
- **`ConsumerCursorStore` gained a default `lastRecoveredFailure(...)` method** (returns empty unless overridden) so a composed store can report an inner-stage failure it chose to recover rather than propagate, without adding a leaky push-callback into the consumer runtime or threading a new argument through `ClusterCursorStore`'s public factory (`AetherNode.java`'s construction call needed zero changes). `ConsumerRuntimeState.observedCommit` now clears the per-consumer failure OPTIMISTICALLY at the start of each attempt (rather than on the outer promise's success) and polls `lastRecoveredFailure(...)` from that same success handler — clearing on success would otherwise erase a recovered failure recorded moments earlier in the same resolution, since a promise's `.recover(...)` side effects are guaranteed to complete before externally-attached `.onSuccess` listeners run.
- **The two failure origins are now distinguishable on the same surface**: `lastCursorCommitFailure` (both the per-partition Management API field and the underlying `ConsumerState` detail) is prefixed `local commit:` when the local write itself failed, or `checkpoint publish:` when the local write succeeded but the consensus publish was the one recovered — an operator reading only the text can tell which write to investigate [verified: `StreamConsumerRuntimeClusterCursorTest` in `aether/node` (the only module where the real `ClusterCursorStore` and the real `StreamConsumerRuntime` are both on the classpath) — a failing consensus publisher leaves the local commit observably successful while the failure lands on the surface with the `checkpoint publish:` text, a never-settling publisher is bounded at the same 5-second close, and a subsequent clean publish clears the recorded detail; `ClusterCursorStoreTest.CommitFanout` pins the store's own recording/clearing/per-key-scoping contract in isolation].
- **Redelivery contract sharpened** in `management-api.md`: on failover to another node the consumer resumes from the last consensus-published checkpoint, not the outgoing node's local cursor — that local cursor is unreadable from any other node — so a lost publish means redelivery from that older, cluster-visible point, at least once.
- **Round 3: the shutdown-bound count no longer double-counts a commit that later also resolves.** A final commit already marked unsettled at the shutdown bound now records one incident, not two, when it goes on to resolve — whether with a genuine local-commit failure or a recovered checkpoint-publish failure. The ERROR log for the late resolution still fires — the exact failure cause is new information even when the count is not [verified: `StreamConsumerRuntimeTest.CursorCommitObservability#close_countsUnsettledCommit_whenFinalCommitNeverSettlesWithinBound` and `StreamConsumerRuntimeClusterCursorTest#close_countsUnsettledCommit_whenConsensusPublishNeverSettlesWithinBound` now assert the count stays at 1 after the late resolution, where it previously reached 2].
- **Round 4: the round-3 dedup flag was scoped to the wrong thing.** It lived on `ConsumerState` — per CONSUMER — while the ruling is per COMMIT, and a periodic `checkpointIfNeeded` commit and a `close()`-time final commit for the same consumer can both be in flight at once (nothing drains an already-issued periodic commit when `close()` starts; it only stops new poll cycles). With one shared flag, whichever of the two commits got reported first silently starved the other: its later resolution still logged ERROR but skipped the counter, so a genuinely distinct failed commit counted zero. The dedup token now lives on the commit itself (`TrackedCommit.reported`, a fresh `AtomicBoolean` minted inside `observedCommit`), and the shutdown bound reports every commit that was in flight at the moment its snapshot is taken — periodic ones included, via a new `inFlightCommits` registry — CASing each one independently: two unsettled commits now produce two increments and two ERROR lines, one per commit, ever. A commit that starts (or restarts, via a periodic checkpoint tripped by a delivery already in flight when `close()` begins) after that snapshot is taken is not bound-reported at all: its own token still lets a genuine later failure or recovered checkpoint publish count it exactly once through `onCursorCommitFailure`/`recordIfRecovered`, but if it never settles it is never counted and simply stays in `inFlightCommits` for the life of the runtime. A commit whose token was already won (by the bound, or by an earlier failure/recovery) logs its later resolution at WARNING ("late resolution of an already-reported cursor commit"), not ERROR, so the log level and the counter always agree [verified: `StreamConsumerRuntimeTest.CursorCommitObservability#close_countsBothUnsettledCommits_whenPeriodicAndFinalCommitShareOneConsumer` — a periodic and a final commit for one consumer, both unresolved at the bound, count as 2, and the periodic commit's later genuine failure does not add a third].
- **CLI: no change** — the Management API's existing `lastCursorCommitFailure` and `cursorCommitFailureCount` fields carry the round-2 detail without any new shape, so no CLI command needed updating.

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #304: node-mode live events never key correctly)

- `events.js` no longer dedups/keys live events on `event.timestamp`. `ClusterEventView` has
  never had a `timestamp` field — its HLC time has always been named `at`
  (`HlcTimestamp`, packed physical-ms/counter), a naming convention shared by every record in
  the `ClusterEvent` sealed interface and predating the `type` discriminator entirely; the
  client-side `timestamp` read was an original wrong assumption, not a later rename. New
  `eventMillis`/`eventKey` helpers read `at` (unpacking `HlcTimestamp.pack`'s physical-ms
  component) when present, falling back to `timestamp` for Forge-mode events that do use that
  field.
  [verified: `ClusterEventKeyContractTest.eventsJs_computesKeyFromAtOrTimestamp_notTimestampAlone`]
- `index.html`'s event-feed template now keys and displays time through the store's
  `eventKey`/`eventMillis` helpers instead of reading `event.timestamp` directly.
  [verified: `ClusterEventKeyContractTest.indexHtml_usesEventKeyHelper_andNeverReadsEventTimestampDirectly`]
- `ClusterEventView`'s wire shape (`at`, never `timestamp`) is pinned both by serialization and
  by reflection on its record components, as a guard against a future accidental rename in
  either direction.
  [verified: `ClusterEventKeyContractTest.clusterEventView_serializesAtField_neverTimestamp`,
  `ClusterEventKeyContractTest.clusterEventView_recordComponents_nameTheTimeFieldAt_notTimestamp`]
- **Out of scope for this fix, re-scope note for #304:** the trace waterfall (`trace-detail`
  component, loaded in `index.html` but never wired to a data source or a click handler) is
  unbuilt. Building it needs: (1) a click/selection handler from the event feed or invocation
  explorer into the component, (2) a server-side trace-fetch endpoint (none of the existing
  `/api/events`-family routes return per-invocation span/trace data), and (3) a waterfall
  rendering layer inside the component — none of which exists today. This is new feature work,
  not a fix, and should be tracked as its own ticket rather than folded back into #304.
  [mechanism: `index.html:512-524` loads the component and never references it again;
  repo-wide grep for a trace-fetch route under `aether/node`'s REST layer finds none]

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #294: polling is not gated to health)

- Every dashboard poll timer (primary status/events/alerts, the secondary fallback timer, and
  the requests store's own timer) now skips its tick while a client-side `degraded` flag is
  set, instead of continuing to poll a backend the operator's own health check has already
  marked unhealthy.
  [verified: `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.appJs_pollingTimers_skipWhenClusterDegraded_backOffToSlowRetryWhenHealthUnknown`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.requestsJs_pollingTimer_skipsWhenDegraded_backsOffToSlowRetryWhenHealthUnknown`]
- The gate is driven by a new, ungated health probe (run on every primary-timer tick so the
  dashboard can detect recovery, not only degradation) keyed semantically on
  `status !== 'healthy'` — there is no literal `"degraded"` wire value in either health shape
  this dashboard talks to.
  [verified: `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.checkHealth_probesVersionedHealthFirst_thenBareHealthFallback_viaProbeHealthNotPlainGet`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.clusterJs_declaresDegradedFlag_defaultingFalse`]
- **Revised after first review:** the probe now tries `GET /api/v1/health` FIRST — the only
  health route the real node's Management API serves, which has migrated ahead of this
  dashboard (`ManagementRoute`, #300) — falling back to bare `GET /health`, what Forge actually
  serves. The first cut probed bare `/health` only, which meant the gate silently never engaged
  against a real node at all (every probe 404'd, `degraded` never left its default). Forge's own
  `HealthResponse` is hardcoded to always report `"healthy"` and can never signal degradation, an
  honest limit on this gate's real-world triggerability against Forge.
  [mechanism: `StatusRoutes.java` bare `/health` route vs. `ManagementServer`'s `/api/v1/health`;
  Forge's `HealthResponse` construction is `new HealthResponse("healthy", ...)` unconditionally]
- **Revised again after second review (a BLOCKING finding): the gate now tracks three states,
  not two.** Round one's fail-open collapsed "probe answered, no route here" and "probe
  unreachable" into the same `degraded = false` — `RestClient.get()` returns an identical `null`
  for a 404 and for a fetch-level network exception, so a total backend outage read exactly like
  a harmless missing health route, the gate cleared, and every OTHER poller resumed hammering a
  dead backend every 2-3s with network-error toasts the 404 suppression never covered — #294's
  own toast storm, reintroduced in the worst case. A new `RestClient.probeHealth()` reports
  reachability separately from the parsed body (any HTTP response, 404 included, marks the probe
  reachable; only a fetch-level exception marks it unreachable), and a pure `decideHealthState()`
  turns two such probes into one of three verdicts:
  - `healthy` — a probe answered `status: "healthy"`, or a probe answered at all with no usable
    health payload (404 on both paths: reachable, just no route here). Fails open, same as round
    one.
  - `degraded` — a probe answered `status: "unhealthy"`.
  - `unknown` — BOTH paths failed with a network-level error. `decideHealthState()`'s unknown
    branch returns `{unknown: true}` with no `degraded` key at all, so a prior `degraded = true`
    verdict is never overwritten by an outage — a total outage on top of a known-degraded cluster
    must not read back as healthy. It clears the moment either probe answers anything, even a
    404. While unknown, every poll timer backs off to a shared slow 10s retry
    (`cluster.unknownRetryDue()`), and `RestClient` routes every network-exception `.catch()`
    through `_reportNetworkFailure()`, which suppresses the toast (warning once instead) for as
    long as `healthUnknown` stays true — an isolated network blip while the server is otherwise
    known-reachable still toasts normally.
  [verified: `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.decideHealthState_reachableWithNoHealthJson_failsOpenToHealthy_neverToDegradedTrue`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.decideHealthState_bothProbesUnreachable_omitsDegradedKeyEntirely_soCallerCannotOverwriteIt`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.checkHealth_unknownBranch_returnsBeforeDegradedAssignment_priorDegradedTrueSurvivesNetworkFailure`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.checkHealth_healthUnknownFlag_assignedUnconditionally_clearsOnAnyAnswerIncluding404`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.clusterJs_declaresHealthUnknownFlag_defaultingFalse_withSharedTenSecondRetryThrottle`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.restClientJs_catchBlocks_routeThroughReportNetworkFailure_notDirectToastPerOccurrence`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.restClientJs_reportNetworkFailure_suppressesToastOnlyWhileHealthUnknown_warnsOnceInstead`,
  `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.restClientJs_probeHealth_neverToasts_reachableMeansAnyHttpResponseNot404Only`]
- A repeat 404 from an endpoint the target server has no route for is now logged once per
  method+path (`console.warn`) instead of toasting on every poll tick; every other failure
  status (5xx, network error while the server is otherwise known-reachable) still toasts on
  every occurrence — a narrow carve-out for the specific, expected case of polling an
  unimplemented endpoint, not general failure suppression.
  [verified: `DashboardPollingGateContractTest.restClientJs_suppressesRepeat404Toasts_logsInstead`]
- **Not in this PR (Forge proxy for the missing endpoints):** 24 REST paths the dashboard calls
  have no matching Forge route today and 404 under Forge (2 more are near-misses mounted under
  a different prefix than the dashboard calls — `/api/thresholds*` vs. Forge's
  `/api/alerts/thresholds*`, and `/api/cluster/topology` vs. Forge's `/api/slices/topology`).
  Every one of these now benefits from the 404-suppression above (logged once, not repeatedly
  toasted), but none is proxied or stubbed by this fix. Full list, each with its calling
  dashboard file: `/api/slices` (app.js), `/api/thresholds`, `/api/thresholds` (POST),
  `/api/thresholds/{metric}` (DELETE) (alerts.js), `/api/controller/config` (GET+POST),
  `/api/ttm/status`, `/api/logging/levels` (GET+POST) (cluster.js), `/api/routes`
  (deployments.js), `/api/cluster/config` (desiredtopology.js), `/api/cluster/governors`,
  `/api/cluster/topology` (governors.js), `/api/invocations/metrics`,
  `/api/invocations/metrics/slow` (requests.js), `/api/schema/status`,
  `/api/schema/retry/{datasource}` (schema.js), `/api/cluster/storage`, `/api/storage`,
  `/api/storage/{name}`, `/api/storage/snapshot/{name}` (storage.js), `/api/deploy`,
  `/api/ab-tests` (strategies.js), `/api/streams` (streams.js).
  [mechanism: cross-referenced every `RestClient.get/post/put/del` call site in the dashboard
  JS against every registered route in Forge's 9 `*Routes.java` files]

### Fixed (2026-09-05 — #292: live alerts never render)

- `app.js` no longer unwraps the WS envelope before dispatching an `ALERT`/`ALERT_RESOLVED`
  message to the alerts store. `AlertManager.buildAlertMessage` puts the `type` discriminator
  at the top level only (`{"type":"ALERT","data":{...}}`), never duplicated inside `data`; the
  old `updateFromWs(data.data || data)` call stripped the envelope before the store ever saw
  `type`, so its `data.type === 'ALERT'` check was always false and nothing rendered.
  [verified: `AlertWsEnvelopeContractTest.appJs_dispatchesWholeEnvelopeToAlertsStore_notUnwrappedPayload`]
- `alerts.js`'s `updateFromWs` now reads the discriminator off the still-wrapped envelope
  (`envelope.type`) and unwraps `data` itself, instead of checking `data.type` on a payload
  that never carried it.
  [verified: `AlertWsEnvelopeContractTest.alertsJs_readsDiscriminatorOnTheEnvelope_notOnTheUnwrappedPayload`]
- The wire shape itself — top-level `type`, alert fields under `data`, never duplicated — is
  pinned against `AlertManager.checkThreshold`'s actual return value (the literal broadcast
  payload, per `DashboardMetricsPublisher.checkAndBroadcastAlerts`), not a hand-written stand-in.
  [verified: `AlertWsEnvelopeContractTest.checkThreshold_valueAboveCritical_returnsEnvelopeWithTopLevelTypeAndUnwrappedData`]
- The alerts store is now also refreshed from the same gated, repeating poll timer that drives
  cluster status and events (`app.js` `startPolling()`), not only once at page load — so a
  missed or dropped WS message self-heals within one poll cycle instead of leaving the panel
  stale until the next alert fires.
  [verified: `AlertWsEnvelopeContractTest.appJs_startPolling_refreshesAlertsStoreOnTheRepeatingTimer_notOnlyOnce`]
- `ALERT_RESOLVED`'s envelope shape (`AlertManager.broadcastAlertResolved`) is a private,
  directly-broadcasting method with no return-value seam to exercise from a test; its shape
  matches `ALERT`'s by source inspection only.
  [design intent — unverified]

### Fixed (2026-09-04 — #855: `aether/node` test-compile broken by three #826-era `ManageableNode` doubles missing `schemaOrchestrator()`)
- **Three hand-written test doubles didn't override the `schemaOrchestrator()` abstract method** added to `ManageableNode` by #543, leaving `aether/node`'s test sources uncompilable on the rc4 tip; the override is added to each, mirroring the existing `unsupported()`-double convention — test-only, no production code changed [verified: `aether/node` full suite, 1132 tests].

### Removed (2026-09-04 — #854: dead `[operations.tls] cluster_secret` bootstrap key)
- **`TlsDeploymentConfig.clusterSecret()` had no live caller** — #824 deleted `DockerComposeGenerator`, its only reader, leaving the accessor unreachable and failing the dead-surface gate. The `cluster_secret` component is removed from `TlsDeploymentConfig`, the `[operations.tls] cluster_secret` TOML key is no longer parsed by `ClusterBootstrapConfigParser`, and the reference docs table drops the row [mechanism: `ConfigKeyLivenessTest.clusterBootstrapConfig_everyAccessor_isReachableExemptOrSuppressed` reflectively scans every config accessor for a live caller, reflective-binding exemption, or `@ConfigKeyLive` suppression].
- **This is unrelated to the live, same-named `cluster_secret`** used for cluster transport trust (`[tls] cluster_secret` / `AETHER_CLUSTER_SECRET`, read by `Main.resolveClusterSecret(TlsConfig)`) and to the CLI's own `BootstrapState.clusterSecret()` bootstrap-anchor field — neither is touched by this change.
- **An `[operations.tls] cluster_secret` line in an existing `aether.toml` is now silently ignored** rather than read into a dead field — `TomlDocument` has no unknown-key rejection anywhere in this parser, so this matches how every other unrecognized key in the file already behaves.

### Fixed (2026-09-04 — #841: ALL-mode scheduled-task counters shared one cluster-wide row instead of one per node)

- **An `execution_mode = "all"` task's `totalExecutions`/`consecutiveFailures`/etc. all accumulated into a single KV entry, even though every quorum member runs its own independent timer for the same task** — two nodes racing a read-modify-write against that one entry could lose one node's update, and the reported total no longer corresponded to any single node's real activity. `ScheduledTaskStateKey` now carries an optional node component: ALL-mode reads and writes are keyed by `ctx.self()`, so each node owns its own row; `execution_mode = "single"` is unchanged, since only the leader ever executes it
  [mechanism: `ScheduledTaskManager.TaskOps.stateKeyFor(ctx, task)` branches on `task.executionMode()`; pinned by `aether/aether-invoke/src/test/java/org/pragmatica/aether/invoke/ScheduledTaskManagerTest.java#MultiNodeStateIsolation` — two manager instances, distinct node ids, sharing one backing map in-process, asserting neither node's count is lost or overwritten by the other; component-level, not a live multi-node run].
- **`GET /api/v1/scheduled-tasks/executions-by-node/...` reported the task's `registeredBy` node as the sole executor for every mode** (an RC1 stub, count = `totalExecutions`). It now aggregates real per-node rows by scanning the live `KVStore` for node-scoped state entries, one row per node that has actually executed, sorted by `nodeId`
  [mechanism: `ScheduledTaskRoutes.buildExecutionsByNode`; pinned by `ScheduledTaskRoutesExecutionsByNodeTest.java#MultipleNodes` and `#WithState`].
- **Rolling-upgrade note:** a pre-#841 global (non-node-scoped) state entry is excluded from the new per-node scan rather than misread as belonging to some node, so an ALL-mode task's per-node counters restart at zero after upgrading instead of continuing from the old shared total
  [mechanism: the scan filters on `key.node().isPresent()` and task identity; pinned by `ScheduledTaskRoutesExecutionsByNodeTest.java#InvalidEntriesExcluded`, which seeds both a pre-#841 global entry for the target task and a node-scoped entry for a different task and asserts both are excluded].
- **`GET /api/v1/scheduled-tasks` (tasks-list summary) and `GET /api/v1/scheduled-tasks/state` (single-task state) also read the unscoped, single-row `ScheduledTaskStateRegistry` mirror regardless of execution mode**, reporting zero/stale totals for an ALL-mode task on the two surfaces `executions-by-node` did not cover. Both now aggregate the same per-node rows via the same `KVStore.forEach` idiom (`totalExecutions`/`skippedOverlaps` summed, `consecutiveFailures`/`lastExecutionAt` max, `nextFireAt` min, `lastFailureMessage`/`updatedAt` from whichever row is freshest by `updatedAt`) [design intent — unverified beyond the field-level reasoning; no review ruling pins these five combine choices specifically, only the two additive fields]
  [mechanism: `ScheduledTaskRoutes.toSummary`/`buildStateResponse` branch on `ExecutionMode.ALL` into `aggregateAllModeState`/`combineNodeStates`; pinned by `ScheduledTaskRoutesAllModeAggregationTest.java` (`ListSummary`, `SingleTaskState`), including a global-shaped-key-exclusion case per surface added after an adversarial mutation probe found the first pass of these tests didn't catch a dropped node-presence filter].
- Docs updated: `aether/docs/reference/management-api.md` (`/trigger` 409 response, per-node aggregation and rolling-upgrade note on all three read surfaces) and `aether/docs/slice-developers/resource-reference.md` (Execution State, Operational Controls).
- **`POST /api/v1/scheduled-tasks/inject` (dev/test-only, `AETHER_INSECURE_DEV_MODE` gated) now keys `all`-mode writes by `ctx.self()` too**, mirroring the automatic path, so an `/inject` call on an `all`-mode task lands on the same per-node row the three read surfaces above aggregate — no longer an orphaned write invisible to the Management API
  [mechanism: `ScheduledTaskRoutes.injectStateKeyFor` branches on `task.executionMode()` exactly like `ScheduledTaskManager.TaskOps#stateKeyFor`; pinned by `ScheduledTaskRoutesInjectTest.java#KeyScoping.inject_onAllModeTask_advancesStateVisibleOnStateEndpoint`, and by `#HappyPath.inject_invokesTask_writesSuccessState_andAdvancesLastExecution` — a mutation probe reverting the branch to the old unscoped key turns both tests red].
- **Remaining caveat, `single`-mode only:** `/inject` still writes the same unscoped key the leader's automatic fire uses, with no `tryClaim`/`release` guard around the read-modify-write — a concurrent writer to that entry between the read and the write is silently lost (`/trigger` writes no state entry at all, so it is not a racer on this key). Unchanged by this fix; a documented TOCTOU limitation of a dev/test-only route, not addressed here.

### Fixed (2026-09-04 — #837: cluster config/status/upgrade against a cluster with no stored config answered 500)

- **`GET /api/v1/cluster/config`, `GET /api/v1/cluster/status`, and `POST /api/v1/cluster/upgrade` against a fresh, unconfigured cluster (e.g. right after a `docker compose down -v` volume wipe) all answered HTTP 500.** The two GETs shared `ClusterConfigRoutes`'s `ConfigNotFoundError` — the same bare, statusless `Cause` #335/#835 traced for `POST /api/v1/cluster/scale` — defaulting to 500 through `ProblemResponses.resolveStatus`. Upgrade routed through the same promise-failing lookup instead of branching on absence.
- **The two reads now answer HTTP 404** (`ConfigNotFoundError` implements `HttpStatusAware`, mapping to `HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND`) — absence of a resource on a GET, not server failure. `GET /api/v1/cluster/status` was considered for a 200 with an explicit "config absent" field instead, and rejected: `ClusterStatusResponse` mixes config-derived fields (`clusterName`, `desiredVersion`, `desiredCoreCount`) with live node/membership data, and fabricating the former or adding a new flag would misrepresent a shape this route has never returned before.
- **Upgrade now refuses with a typed `ClusterConfigError.NoConfigToUpgrade`, HTTP 409**, mirroring #335/#835's `NoConfigToScale`: an `UpgradeRequest` carries only `targetVersion`, not the cluster name, topology, or deployment settings a config requires, so there is no honest way to synthesize one. The response names the actual recovery (`aether cluster bootstrap <aether-cluster.toml>`, then retry the upgrade) [verified: aether/node/src/test/java/org/pragmatica/aether/api/routes/ClusterConfigRoutesNoConfigTest.java].
- **`aether/tests/integration/lib/cluster.sh`'s `scale_cluster` chaos helper** previously logged every non-2xx scale response identically, body truncated and unparsed. It now extracts and prints the RFC 9457 `detail` field via a new `_extract_problem_detail` helper (jq with a grep/sed fallback) and labels 404/409 as an expected typed refusal versus a genuine failure for any other status [mechanism: cluster.sh non-2xx branch, no change to the function's return code].
- Docs updated: `management-api.md` gains a "Not Found (404)" note under `GET /api/v1/cluster/config` and `GET /api/v1/cluster/status`, and a "Conflicts (HTTP 409)" note under `POST /api/v1/cluster/upgrade`, each naming the recovery command [mechanism: docs cross-checked against the message text the route emits].

### Changed (2026-09-04 — #819: per-PR changelog fragments assembled at release prep)
- **`CHANGELOG.md` is no longer edited by feature pull requests.** Each pull request adds
  `changelog.d/<number>-<slug>.md` holding its entry in the existing format;
  `scripts/changelog-assemble.sh` folds the fragments into the `Unreleased` section at release prep.
  Every rc4 pull request had been conflicting on the one file all of them appended to.
- **A CI check** (`.github/workflows/changelog.yml`, `scripts/changelog-check.sh`) fails a pull request
  that edits `CHANGELOG.md` without the `release-prep` label, or that changes sources without a
  well-formed fragment and without the `no-changelog` label. Documentation-only pull requests are exempt.

### Fixed (2026-09-04 — #783: `content` storage instance bypassed demotion/GC and could never be encrypted)

- **`StorageFactory.defaultContentStorage(Option<DHTClient>)` built the `content` `StorageInstance` (the shared per-node instance `ContentStore` resources provision through) entirely outside `storageSetups` — no `MetadataStore`, no `DemotionManager`, no `StorageGarbageCollector` — so `StorageMaintenanceDriver` (#250/#803, ticks every registered `StorageSetup`) never reached it and memory usage grew unbounded.** The same bypass also kept `content` out of the config-aware, keyring-aware `createAll`/`createOne` path (#253), so it could never be encrypted regardless of `[storage.encryption]` — #830 shipped a boot-time WARN naming this gap. `defaultContentStorage` is deleted; `createAll` now synthesizes a `content` entry through `createOne`, mirroring the synthesized `artifacts` default from #830, whenever `[storage.content]` isn't explicit. One behaviour change this carries for operators who already HAD an explicit `[storage.content]` section: before this fix `createAll` built that section's setup but `AetherNode` ignored it and handed `ContentStore` the bare instance, so the section was inert for `ContentStore`; after it, the section governs `ContentStore` — a stray `memory_max_bytes`, `encrypted = true` or path in it takes effect on upgrade
  [mechanism: `StorageFactory.createAll` — `if (!configs.containsKey(CONTENT_NAME))` branch; `AetherNode` reads `storageSetups.get("content").instance()` in place of the old `defaultContentStorage` call — that hand-off is pinned through a REAL BOOT by `AetherNodeContentStorageWiringBootTest#assembleNode_registersContentSetupInstance_asTheSpiStorageInstanceExtension`: the `StorageInstance` extension the node's `SpiResourceProvider` hands every factory (`ContentStoreFactory` included) `isSameAs` `node.storageSetups().get("content").instance()` and is not `artifacts`'. Red-before is review probe F — `registerRuntimeExtensions(..., artifactStorage)` at the call site — which left all 1166 `aether/node` tests green until this test existed (review round 2, BLOCKING 2); verified, in-JVM through the real `StorageFactory` + real composite managers + real `StorageMaintenanceDriver` (not multi-node): `StorageMaintenanceWiringTest#createAll_realMaintenanceDriverTick_reachesSynthesizedContentInstance` pins REGISTRATION and the #250 shared-DHT guard; `#createAll_realMaintenanceDriverTick_actuallyShrinksContentMemoryTier` pins that the memory cache ACTUALLY shrinks across one tick (memory-tier residency measured before/after from content's own `MetadataStore`, plus content's own `DemotionManager.stats().bytesMoved()`); `#createAll_realMaintenanceDriverTick_actuallyCollectsOrphanedContentBlock` pins that an orphaned block is ACTUALLY collected (disk file gone from the filesystem, lifecycle record gone, block unreadable). Mutation-probed: cutting `demotionManager.demote()` out of `StorageMaintenanceDriver.tick()` reddens ONLY the demotion test, and cutting `garbageCollector.collectGarbage()` reddens ONLY the GC test -- each pins its own property and neither is satisfied by the other's work]. Every instrument reads content's OWN manager, never the composite — a composite counter could be satisfied entirely by `artifacts`.
- **`content` is now encrypted whenever `[storage.encryption]` is configured with a resolvable keyring, and stays plaintext otherwise, with no explicit `[storage.content]` section required** — `encrypted = keyring.isPresent()`, same rule as the synthesized `artifacts` default
  [verified: `StorageFactoryEncryptionTest#createAll_synthesizedDefaultContent_isEncrypted_whenKeyringPresent` / `#createAll_synthesizedDefaultContent_staysPlaintext_whenKeyringAbsent`].
- **#830's boot-time WARN ("'content' storage instance is NOT covered") no longer fires** — content is covered like every other instance now
  [verified: `AetherNodeContentStorageWarnBootTest#assembleNode_doesNotWarnOnContentStorage_whenKeyringConfigured`, a real boot on ephemeral ports with log4j appender interception; red-before is re-adding the retired WARN call].
- **The synthesized default's disk/snapshot paths are siblings of the synthesized `artifacts` default** (`artifactsDiskPath.resolveSibling("content")`, then `/blocks` and `/snapshots` — the same convention `streamDataDir` already uses), never the bare `StorageConfig.storageConfig()` default — reusing that bare default verbatim would have collided both instances' snapshot files (and disk blocks) in the same directory, since `assembleSetup` reads `snapshotPath` with no per-instance subdirectory of its own
  [verified: `StorageFactoryEncryptionTest#createAll_synthesizedContent_usesSiblingDiskPath_distinctFromArtifacts` — two synthesized instances, distinct `basePath`s through the real factory; since review round 2 it also `forceSnapshot`s content and asserts the file lands under the sibling `content/snapshots`, so both halves of the derivation have a red-on-revert: `defaults.diskPath()` in place of `content/blocks` reddens it (probe H), and `defaults.snapshotPath()` in place of `content/snapshots` reddens it too].
- **The DHT tier keeps the `content-blocks` key prefix**, so a block written under the old bypass path stays reachable through the new instance — `buildTiers` derives `dhtKeyPrefix = name + "-blocks"` from the instance name `"content"`, reproducing the old hardcoded prefix exactly, with no code change needed
  [verified: `StorageFactoryEncryptionTest#createAll_synthesizedContent_readsPreExistingBlock_underOldContentBlocksDhtPrefix` — seeds a block under `content-blocks/<id>` directly, reads it back through the new synthesized instance].
- **Tier sizes:** `content`'s memory tier stays at 256 MB (`memory_max_bytes`, unchanged from the old bypass default) plus the optional DHT tier (unchanged); it now additionally gets a 10 GB disk tier (`disk_max_bytes`) between them — the old bypass path had no disk tier at all, so this is new capacity and new coverage, not a regression of the memory ceiling.
- Docs updated to drop the now-resolved content-encryption/demotion-GC exclusion: `known-limitations.md`, `configuration.md` (storage-encryption coverage section), `feature-catalog.md` row 207 (Hierarchical Storage Engine).
- **Known limitation carried forward, filed separately by the reviewer:** any two explicitly-configured `[storage.X]` sections that both omit `disk_path`/`snapshot_path` still collide on the bare default (`/data/aether/storage`), and `LocalDiskTier.calculateUsedBytes()` double-counts across them — this fix's sibling-path derivation only covers the *synthesized* `artifacts`/`content` defaults, not explicit sections. No data loss (GC/demotion are `MetadataStore`-driven, not directory-scan-driven) — an accounting-only hazard.
- **Scope boundary — #812:** `DefaultContentStore`'s write path (`putDirect`/`storeManifestAndCreateRef`) pairs `storage.put()` with `storage.createRef()`, the exact double-count pattern #812 tracks — a written-then-deleted content block never reaches `refCount == 0`. Before this fix that bug was inert for `content` (nothing ever ran GC against it); after this fix, GC now runs but will not actually collect an orphaned content block until #812 lands. Not fixed here.

### Findings surfaced by this fix, NOT fixed here

- **`createAll` is not atomic with respect to on-disk encryption markers.** When one instance fails to
  construct, instances built before it keep whatever `EncryptingStorageTier.wrapLocalDisk` already
  stamped on their directories. A later keyring-less boot then refuses on a `.encryption-enabled`
  marker for a directory that never received a single ciphertext block. This predates #783 — it
  already applied to the synthesized `artifacts` default whenever no explicit `[storage.artifacts]`
  section is configured — and #783 only widens the population it can bite by adding `content`. It is
  the disk-side twin of the DHT-side hazard #858 removed structurally. Not fixed here: the remedy sits
  in #253/#858/#831's marker lifecycle, not in this ticket's wiring change
  [evidence: `StorageFactoryEncryptionTest#createAll_leavesNoDhtMarker_whenDiskGuardRefusesBeforeDhtEncryptionIsApplied`
  needed an explicit `[storage.content]` entry after this change, exactly as it already needed one for
  `artifacts`, and for the identical reason — the comment there records it].
- **A written-but-never-read block was invisible to demotion — true when this fragment was first
  written, FIXED by #886 (PR #901) before this landed.** An earlier revision of this bullet reported
  the defect as open, and gave the wrong mechanism (it blamed `computeLifecycle`'s `computeIfPresent`
  dropping the promotion record; #886 shows the record was present and was lost to `trackNewBlock`'s
  unconditional re-create one step later). #901 merged onto the release branch first; its fragment,
  `changelog.d/886-write-only-block-demotion.md`, is authoritative for the defect and the mechanism,
  and this entry no longer claims anything about either. What changed HERE as a consequence: the
  demotion test used to fill content's memory tier write-then-read because the read was the only way
  a written block became visible to the demoter, and its `fillMemoryTier` javadoc called that read
  "REQUIRED". The read is dropped, not kept — a write-only fill is the workload acceptance item 3
  asks about, and a retained read would keep that test green through a regression of #886 while
  claiming to measure normal use. Pinned: with `trackNewBlock` mutated back to the unconditional
  `createLifecycle`, `actuallyShrinksContentMemoryTier`'s baseline (`memoryBefore == 8`) goes red
  (0 listed), so the demotion test now also depends on #886's fix and says so
  [verified: `StorageMaintenanceWiringTest#fillMemoryTier`, write-only since review round 2; the reviewer's
  probe G (read removed on the merged tree, before this change) was the positive control that the read
  was no longer needed — 0 red of 8].
- **Ticket wording vs. shipped behaviour:** acceptance item 3 asks that "orphaned DHT blocks are
  actually collected". They are deliberately NOT — `DefaultStorageGarbageCollector.deleteBlock` calls
  `StorageInstance.deleteFromPrivateTiers`, never `delete`, precisely so this node's local refcount
  cannot delete a block another node may still reference (#250's guard). Collection is a private-tier
  operation by design; the tests pin that, not the ticket's phrasing.
